entries.story: Proto-Semitic *ṯ. Arabic kept it as ث. Aramaic shifted to plain t. Hebrew shifted to ש. Same root, three different fates — and when Aramaic and Arabic stand together, Hebrew is the outlier.

tafsir_first.hebrew_phrase: וַיִּתְהַלֵּךְ חֲנוֹךְ אֶת-הָאֱלֹהִים אַחֲרֵי הוֹלִידוֹ אֶת-מְתוּשֶׁלַח שְׁלֹשׁ…

entries.story: Same *ṯ shift. The Arabic dual ending -ayn matches the Aramaic -ēn ending exactly. Hebrew's -ayim is a related dual — the morphology agrees across all three, but only Arabic and Aramaic kept the consonant.

tafsir_first.hebrew_phrase: וַיְחִי-יֶרֶד שְׁתַּיִם וְשִׁשִּׁים שָׁנָה וּמְאַת שָׁנָה וַיּוֹלֶד אֶת-חֲנוֹךְ

entries.story: Hebrew shōr, Aramaic tōr, Arabic ṯawr — same beast, same word, three different sibilants. The constellation Taurus is the same word: 'the bull.'

tafsir_first.hebrew_phrase: וְכִי-יִגַּח שׁוֹר אֶת-אִישׁ אוֹ אֶת-אִשָּׁה וָמֵת--סָקוֹל יִסָּקֵל הַשּׁוֹר…

entries.story: Proto-Semitic *ḏ. Arabic kept it as ذ. Aramaic shifted to d. Hebrew shifted to ז. Modern Arabic ḏahab and Onkelos' dəhab are still recognizably the same word.
entries.onkelos_phrase_en: and the gold of that land is good

tafsir_first.hebrew_phrase: שֵׁם הָאֶחָד פִּישׁוֹן--הוּא הַסֹּבֵב אֵת כָּל-אֶרֶץ הַחֲוִילָה אֲשֶׁר-שָׁם…

entries.story: The same *ḏ shift again. The verb for ritual slaughter — kosher and ḥalāl alike use this one root: ḏabaḥ in Arabic, dəbaḥ in Onkelos, zāvaḥ in the Torah.
entries.onkelos_phrase_en: and the sacrifice shall be upon it (the altar)

tafsir_first.hebrew_phrase: זֹבֵחַ לָאֱלֹהִים יָחֳרָם--בִּלְתִּי לַיהוָה לְבַדּוֹ

entries.story: *ḏ → Aramaic d, Hebrew ז, Arabic ḏ. Aramaic and Arabic are almost identical: udnā / uḏun. Hebrew ozen took the third path.
entries.onkelos_phrase_en: his master shall pierce his ear with the awl

tafsir_first.ja_phrase: אד'ן נור אללה פי הד'א אלמוצ'ע
tafsir_first.hebrew_phrase: וַיִּיקַץ יַעֲקֹב מִשְּׁנָתוֹ וַיֹּאמֶר אָכֵן יֵשׁ יְהוָה בַּמָּקוֹם הַזֶּה…

entries.story: Proto-Semitic *ṣ́ (an emphatic lateral, gone from every modern language). Arabic became ض. Aramaic became ע. Hebrew became צ. Same word: earth/land.

tafsir_first.hebrew_phrase: בְּרֵאשִׁית בָּרָא אֱלֹהִים אֵת הַשָּׁמַיִם וְאֵת הָאָרֶץ

entries.story: One root, two senses across all three languages: 'male' and 'remember.' (To name a son was to keep the name alive.) Same *ḏ split: Arabic ذ, Aramaic d, Hebrew ז.

tafsir_first.hebrew_phrase: וַיִּבְרָא אֱלֹהִים אֶת-הָאָדָם בְּצַלְמוֹ בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים בָּרָא אֹתוֹ זָכָר…

entries.story: M-L-K. Three letters, same meaning across all Semitic languages. The Hebrew name Malki-tzedek and the Arabic name Malik are the same word.
entries.onkelos_phrase_en: and kings who rule over peoples shall come from you

tafsir_first.ja_phrase: אול מן סכן אלאכ'ביה ומלך אלמאשיה
tafsir_first.hebrew_phrase: וַתֵּלֶד עָדָה אֶת-יָבָל הוּא הָיָה--אֲבִי יֹשֵׁב אֹהֶל וּמִקְנֶה

entries.story: The greeting that crosses every border. Shalom, shlām, salām — same root, same wish, three pronunciations.

tafsir_first.hebrew_phrase: וּמַלְכִּי-צֶדֶק מֶלֶךְ שָׁלֵם הוֹצִיא לֶחֶם וָיָיִן וְהוּא כֹהֵן לְאֵל עֶלְיוֹן

entries.story: Arabic sifr specifically means a book of scripture — the Quran calls the books of the Torah 'al-asfār.' Same word as the Torah's own ספר.
entries.onkelos_phrase_en: this is the book of the generations of Adam

tafsir_first.hebrew_phrase: דַּבֵּר אֶל-בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל לֵאמֹר אִישׁ אִישׁ כִּי-יִהְיֶה-טָמֵא לָנֶפֶשׁ…

entries.story: K-T-B. The verb 'to write' is identical in all three. A kātib in Arabic is a scribe — the same act as a Hebrew sofer's.

tafsir_first.hebrew_phrase: וַיְהִי-שָׁם עִם-יְהוָה אַרְבָּעִים יוֹם וְאַרְבָּעִים לַיְלָה--לֶחֶם לֹא אָכַל…

entries.story: Navi, nəviyyā, nabī. The same word the Quran uses for Mūsā and Ibrāhīm. The root is shared with Akkadian — a 'called one,' summoned to speak.

tafsir_first.ja_phrase: ואלאן ארדד זוגה' אלרגל אנה נבי
tafsir_first.hebrew_phrase: וְעַתָּה הָשֵׁב אֵשֶׁת-הָאִישׁ כִּי-נָבִיא הוּא וְיִתְפַּלֵּל בַּעַדְךָ וֶחְיֵה…

entries.story: Kohen, kāhanā, kāhin. The Arabic word kept the older meaning of seer/diviner; the Hebrew specialized to Temple service. The Quran uses kāhin for pre-Islamic Arabian priests.
The verb Israel is called to recite twice daily. In Arabic prayer: samiʿa Allāhu liman ḥamidah — 'God hears whoever praises Him.' Same root, same theology.

tafsir_first.hebrew_phrase: וַיִּשְׁמַע אַבְרָם כִּי נִשְׁבָּה אָחִיו וַיָּרֶק אֶת-חֲנִיכָיו יְלִידֵי…

entries.story: Q-R-ʾ. The root behind both 'Quran' (the recitation) and the Torah's mikra (the reading). Aramaic qrā means both call and read.

tafsir_first.hebrew_phrase: וַיָּשִׂימוּ עָלָיו שָׂרֵי מִסִּים לְמַעַן עַנֹּתוֹ בְּסִבְלֹתָם וַיִּבֶן עָרֵי…

entries.story: A false friend in the making. Hebrew and Aramaic both mean 'said.' Arabic amara shifted to 'commanded.' But the root is one, and Quran/Torah readers meet it daily.

tafsir_first.hebrew_phrase: וַיֹּאמֶר הָאָדָם זֹאת הַפַּעַם עֶצֶם מֵעֲצָמַי וּבָשָׂר מִבְּשָׂרִי לְזֹאת…

entries.story: Identical letters in all three. Hebrew/Aramaic dīn = law, judgment. Arabic dīn shifted to 'religion' (the law one follows). Yawm al-dīn = day of judgment.

tafsir_first.ja_phrase: אכ'רג אנת וגמיע אלקום אלדין מעך
tafsir_first.hebrew_phrase: וְיָרְדוּ כָל-עֲבָדֶיךָ אֵלֶּה אֵלַי וְהִשְׁתַּחֲווּ-לִי לֵאמֹר צֵא אַתָּה…

entries.story: Ḥ-K-M. A Hakham, a Hakim — same word, two cultures using the same title for sages, judges, and physicians.

tafsir_first.hebrew_phrase: וְאַתָּה תְּדַבֵּר אֶל-כָּל-חַכְמֵי-לֵב אֲשֶׁר מִלֵּאתִיו רוּחַ חָכְמָה…

entries.story: Hebrew/Aramaic olam = forever, eternity. Arabic ʿālam shifted to 'world.' Both senses converge in the medieval phrase olam ha-zeh / al-ʿālam — 'this world.'

tafsir_first.hebrew_phrase: כִּי יֹדֵעַ אֱלֹהִים כִּי בְּיוֹם אֲכָלְכֶם מִמֶּנּוּ וְנִפְקְחוּ עֵינֵיכֶם…

entries.story: Eved / ʿabd. Same word — and the same theology: a worshipper of God is His servant. The names Ovadia and ʿAbdallāh are the same name.

tafsir_first.hebrew_phrase: וַיֹּאמֶר אֵלָיו הָעֶבֶד אוּלַי לֹא-תֹאבֶה הָאִשָּׁה לָלֶכֶת אַחֲרַי…

entries.story: Hebrew uses hitpallel. Aramaic and Arabic share צלי / ṣallā — to pray. The Muslim ṣalāh and the Aramaic tzlota are the same word; Onkelos uses tzlī wherever the Torah says hitpallel.

tafsir_first.ja_phrase: הודי' צראך' בני אסראיל קד וצל
tafsir_first.hebrew_phrase: וְעַתָּה הִנֵּה צַעֲקַת בְּנֵי-יִשְׂרָאֵל בָּאָה אֵלָי וְגַם-רָאִיתִי…

entries.story: Aramaic səgīd = Arabic sajada — the verb at the root of masjid (mosque) and sajdah (prostration). Onkelos uses סגד for Hebrew hishtaḥavah throughout.
entries.onkelos_phrase_en: and he bowed to the ground

tafsir_first.hebrew_phrase: וַיִּשָּׂא עֵינָיו וַיַּרְא וְהִנֵּה שְׁלֹשָׁה אֲנָשִׁים נִצָּבִים עָלָיו…

entries.story: B-Y-T. The most ordinary word. A bayit is a bayt is a beita. Bethlehem = bayt laḥm, 'house of bread.'
entries.onkelos_phrase_en: to the house of your servant

tafsir_first.ja_phrase: אמץ' מן ארצ'ך ומולדך ובית אביך
tafsir_first.hebrew_phrase: וַיֹּאמֶר יְהוָה אֶל-אַבְרָם לֶךְ-לְךָ מֵאַרְצְךָ וּמִמּוֹלַדְתְּךָ וּמִבֵּית…

entries.story: Yad, yad, yad. The most stable body-part word across Semitic. Yedidya = beloved of God; ya yedi in colloquial Arabic = 'O my hand!' — an exclamation.

tafsir_first.hebrew_phrase: וְאַךְ אֶת-דִּמְכֶם לְנַפְשֹׁתֵיכֶם אֶדְרֹשׁ מִיַּד כָּל-חַיָּה אֶדְרְשֶׁנּוּ…

entries.story: Rosh / resh / raʾs. Also: 'leader' in all three (rosh ha-yeshiva, raʾīs). The letter ר / ر itself is named after this word.
entries.onkelos_phrase_en: and Israel bowed at the head of the bed

tafsir_first.hebrew_phrase: וְאֵיבָה אָשִׁית בֵּינְךָ וּבֵין הָאִשָּׁה וּבֵין זַרְעֲךָ וּבֵין זַרְעָהּ הוּא…

entries.story: ʿAyin / ʿayn means both 'eye' and 'water-spring' in all three — the metaphor (springs as the earth's eyes) is older than any of the languages.

tafsir_first.hebrew_phrase: וַיָּשֻׁבוּ וַיָּבֹאוּ אֶל-עֵין מִשְׁפָּט הִוא קָדֵשׁ וַיַּכּוּ אֶת-כָּל-שְׂדֵה…

entries.story: Lisan al-ʿArab is the great medieval Arabic dictionary; leshon ha-kodesh is Hebrew's name for itself. Same root, same metaphor: the language is the tongue.
Hebrew uses yayin — but Aramaic and Arabic share the OTHER Semitic root for wine: ḥamar / khamr. Onkelos always translates יין as חמרא, the exact Arabic word.

tafsir_first.hebrew_phrase: וַיֵּשְׁתְּ מִן-הַיַּיִן וַיִּשְׁכָּר וַיִּתְגַּל בְּתוֹךְ אָהֳלֹה

entries.story: Nahar, nahrā, nahr. The four rivers of Eden and the Nahr al-Furāt (Euphrates) carry the same word.

tafsir_first.hebrew_phrase: וְנָהָר יֹצֵא מֵעֵדֶן לְהַשְׁקוֹת אֶת-הַגָּן וּמִשָּׁם יִפָּרֵד וְהָיָה…

entries.story: ʾ-K-L. Eat. The noun forms maʾakhal (food) and maʾkūl share the same root and the same morphological pattern.

tafsir_first.hebrew_phrase: וַתֵּרֶא הָאִשָּׁה כִּי טוֹב הָעֵץ לְמַאֲכָל וְכִי תַאֲוָה-הוּא לָעֵינַיִם…

entries.story: Q-W-M. Talitha kumi (girl, arise) is famous from the Gospels — the same verb as Arabic qāma yaqūm. Islamic prayer opens with qiyām, the standing.

tafsir_first.hebrew_phrase: וַיֹּאמֶר קַיִן אֶל-הֶבֶל אָחִיו וַיְהִי בִּהְיוֹתָם בַּשָּׂדֶה וַיָּקָם קַיִן…

entries.story: Mūt, māta, mēt. The verb 'to die' is one of the oldest stable Semitic words. Arabic mayyit = corpse.

tafsir_first.hebrew_phrase: וַיִּהְיוּ כָּל-יְמֵי אָדָם אֲשֶׁר-חַי תְּשַׁע מֵאוֹת שָׁנָה וּשְׁלֹשִׁים…

entries.story: L'chaim / la-ḥayāt — to life. The Arabic blessing ḥayyāka Allāh = 'may God give you life.' Eve's name in Genesis (חוה) is from this root in all three languages.
entries.onkelos_phrase_en: all the days of Adam that he lived

tafsir_first.hebrew_phrase: וַיֹּאמֶר אֱלֹהִים--יִשְׁרְצוּ הַמַּיִם שֶׁרֶץ נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה וְעוֹף יְעוֹפֵף…

entries.story: Shem / shmā / ism. The opening word of every Quran chapter — bismillāh (b-ism-Allāh, 'in the name of God') — uses the same word Onkelos uses for Hebrew shem.

tafsir_first.hebrew_phrase: שֵׁם הָאֶחָד פִּישׁוֹן--הוּא הַסֹּבֵב אֵת כָּל-אֶרֶץ הַחֲוִילָה אֲשֶׁר-שָׁם…

entries.story: A Talmudic-Aramaic word for shop/tavern — and Maghrebi Arabic ḥānūt means exactly the same thing. The word migrated with merchants across the medieval Mediterranean.
Shtar (Talmudic for a written contract) shares its root with Arabic saṭr — 'a line' or 'a written line.' A Jewish marriage contract is a shtar; an Arabic line of poetry is a saṭr.

tafsir_first.hebrew_phrase: וַיִּקַּח-לוֹ אֶת-כָּל-אֵלֶּה וַיְבַתֵּר אֹתָם בַּתָּוֶךְ וַיִּתֵּן…

entries.story: Talmudic Aramaic לית = Arabic laysa = 'is not.' Hebrew uses אין. The proverb 'leit din v'leit dayan' (there is no judgment, there is no Judge) is built on this word.

tafsir_first.hebrew_phrase: וַתְּהִי שָׂרַי עֲקָרָה אֵין לָהּ וָלָד

entries.story: Talmudic mārē (and Marana-tha, 'our Lord, come') shares its root with Arabic mawlā — 'lord, patron.' Onkelos uses רבון for אדון; mārē is the rabbinic-Aramaic word.

tafsir_first.hebrew_phrase: יַעַבְדוּךָ עַמִּים וישתחו (וְיִשְׁתַּחֲווּ) לְךָ לְאֻמִּים--הֱוֵה גְבִיר…

entries.story: Same root as sefer (book). Arabic safīr came to mean 'ambassador' (one who carries letters across borders). The connection: it all turns on a written document going somewhere.
